lessons.title: What is a foul
lessons.objective: You can explain what makes contact a foul and what the restart is.

payload.prompt: A defender kicks the attacker's leg while going for the ball. Foul?

scene.alt: A defender's foot makes contact with an attacker's leg; the defender did not get the ball first.

explanation.correct: Yes. If the defender's leg catches the attacker without getting the ball first, that's careless contact and a foul.
explanation.incorrect: Contact that is careless or reckless without getting the ball is a foul. Effort counts if you get the ball clean.
explanation.sayThisLine: Didn't get the ball, just took the leg. That's a foul.

payload.prompt: A defender commits a direct free kick foul inside his own penalty area. What is the restart?

options.text: Indirect free kick
Direct free kick
Penalty kick

explanation.correct: Right. A direct free kick offence by the defending team inside its own penalty area is punished with a penalty kick from the spot.
explanation.incorrect: When a defending player commits a direct free kick offence inside his own penalty area, the restart is a penalty kick rather than a free kick.
explanation.sayThisLine: In the box, it's a penalty. Outside, it's a free kick.

payload.prompt: A striker pushes a centre-back in the back with both hands. Foul?

scene.alt: A forward extends both arms and pushes a defender in the shoulders from behind while neither is competing for the ball.

explanation.correct: Yes. Pushing an opponent is a direct free kick offence when it is careless, reckless or uses excessive force, and shoving someone in the back off the ball is clearly that.
explanation.incorrect: Pushing an opponent, especially from behind and away from the ball, is a foul. It is a direct free kick, or a penalty if it happens in the box.
explanation.sayThisLine: Shoving someone off the ball is a foul, plain and simple.

payload.prompt: Complete the free-kick rule.
payload.template: From a {{direct}} free kick you can score straight away, but from an {{indirect}} free kick another player must touch the ball first.

explanation.correct: Right. A direct free kick can go straight into the net; an indirect one needs a second touch first. The name gives you the clue.
explanation.incorrect: A direct free kick can score directly. An indirect free kick must touch another player before a goal counts, and the referee signals it with a raised arm.
explanation.sayThisLine: Direct free kicks go straight in if you bend it right.

payload.prompt: A defender's hand touches the ball on purpose while trying to stop a shot. Foul?

scene.alt: A defender deliberately puts a hand in front of a shot attempt to block it; the hand contact is clear and intentional.

explanation.correct: Yes. Deliberately using the hand or arm to stop the ball is handball, a direct free kick, or a penalty if it happens in the defender's own box.
explanation.incorrect: Deliberately putting a hand in the way of a shot is handball. Intent is clear here, so it is a foul and, in the box, a penalty.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hand to the shot on purpose, that's a foul.

payload.prompt: A defender's leg trips an attacker who is running away. Is it a foul?

options.text: No, he was running away so it's not serious
Yes, any trip is a foul regardless of direction
Only if the defender meant it

explanation.correct: Right. A trip is a foul whether the attacker is coming at you or running away.
explanation.incorrect: Any trip is a foul. The direction does not matter; the contact does.
explanation.sayThisLine: Tripped is tripped, that's the rule.

statement.speaker: Jamie
statement.text: That wasn't even contact, he just slowed down.

payload.question: What does Jamie think?

options.text: There was no contact so there's no foul
The referee made a bad call
Someone fouled someone
It was a careless kick

payload.translation: Jamie is saying the contact was minimal or didn't happen, so it shouldn't have been called a foul.

followUps.line: Did it look like a dive to you?
followUps.why: Asks if the attacker exaggerated contact.

followUps.line: Did you see the contact in slow motion?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you didn't see the contact clearly, ask what Jamie saw.

lessons.title: Yellow, red and second yellow
lessons.objective: You can explain the difference between a caution and a sending-off.

payload.prompt: Match the card to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A caution for bad behaviour; two yellows in one match mean a red and a sending-off.
A sending-off for serious foul play or violent conduct; the player is off immediately.
A second caution in the same match results in a red and the player leaves the field.

explanation.summary: Yellow warns; two yellows or one serious offence and the player is sent off.
explanation.sayThisLine: Two yellows is a red, one red is off.

payload.prompt: Match the offence to how the referee treats it.

pairs.definition: Repeated fouls after warnings earn a yellow card
Shouting at or abusing the referee earns a yellow card
Punching, spitting or lashing out earns a straight red
A dangerous, over-the-top challenge earns a straight red

explanation.summary: Yellow cards are for repeated or disrespectful behaviour. Red cards are for violence or dangerous challenges that put an opponent at risk.
explanation.sayThisLine: That is a yellow for dissent, but the lunge is a straight red.

payload.prompt: A player gets a yellow in the 30th minute and another yellow in the 75th. Is he sent off?

scene.alt: A player receives a yellow card in the first half and another yellow card in the second half of the same match.

explanation.correct: Yes. Two yellows in the same match is a red card and the player is off.
explanation.incorrect: Two cautions in one match result in a red and an immediate sending-off.
explanation.sayThisLine: Two yellows, automatic red, he's gone.

payload.prompt: A player punches an opponent in the face. What does the referee do?

options.text: Shows a yellow card
Shows a red card immediately
Stops the game and talks to him

explanation.correct: Right. Violent conduct is a direct red; he's off immediately without a yellow first.
explanation.incorrect: Any violent act is a straight red card, no warning. That is the most serious offence.
explanation.sayThisLine: Violent conduct, straight red, no yellow.

statement.speaker: Ava
statement.text: That was a red all day. He jumped on him with both feet.

payload.question: What is Ava saying?

options.text: It was serious foul play, so it deserves a straight red
The referee should send him off immediately
She thinks it was a normal, fair tackle
He should get a yellow for talking back

payload.translation: Ava is saying the challenge was dangerous, jumping in with both feet, so it should be a direct red card and an immediate sending-off.

followUps.line: Did you see it live or in replay?
followUps.why: Asks where she got the angle.

followUps.line: Do you think VAR would intervene?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you're not sure what happened, ask Ava what she saw.

lessons.title: Advantage and tactical fouls
lessons.objective: You can explain why the referee sometimes lets play run and why fans respect a smart foul.

payload.prompt: A midfielder fouls an attacker, but the attacker's teammate is clean through on goal. Does the ref play advantage?

scene.alt: A foul occurs, but the fouled player's team immediately has a scoring opportunity with an open path to goal.

explanation.correct: Yes. The attacker's team benefits more from playing on than from a free kick.
explanation.incorrect: Advantage means the fouled team gets a better opportunity if play continues, so the ref lets it run.
explanation.sayThisLine: Advantage played, they're in a better position now.

payload.prompt: The ref plays advantage, but the fouled team loses the ball within a couple of seconds. What happens?

options.text: The ref stops play and awards the original free kick
Play continues with no free kick
The ref only stops play if there's a foul

explanation.correct: Right. If the expected advantage does not develop within a few seconds, the referee can come back and give the original foul. Once the advantage has clearly developed, there is no going back.
explanation.incorrect: Advantage only stands if it really helps the fouled team. If it fizzles out within a few seconds, the referee can stop play and award the original free kick.
explanation.sayThisLine: Advantage didn't come off, so he's going back for the free kick.

payload.prompt: A defender sees a 3-on-1 break, so he trips the attacker. It stops the counter. Does he get a yellow?

scene.alt: With defenders out of position and attackers on a fast break, a defender deliberately fouls to stop the attack and accepts the yellow card.

explanation.correct: Yes. A tactical foul to stop a dangerous counter gets a yellow, and fans respect the trade-off.
explanation.incorrect: A deliberate foul to break up a counter is a yellow card, but it is often praised as smart defending.
explanation.sayThisLine: Smart foul, takes the yellow to stop the goal chance.

payload.prompt: Two players jump for a header and their shoulders meet. Is it a foul?

options.text: Always a foul, no contact in the air
Only a foul if he uses both arms
Part of the game if both jump for it

explanation.correct: Right. Shoulder-to-shoulder contact when both compete fairly is part of the game.
explanation.incorrect: When both players jump for the ball and use the shoulder fairly, it is legal contest.
explanation.sayThisLine: Both jumped, both fair, no foul.

statement.speaker: Lee
statement.text: Great tactical foul, stopped them on a break for a yellow. That's defending.

payload.question: What does Lee mean?

options.text: The defender deliberately fouled to stop a counter-attack
The defender got a yellow but prevented a goal chance
It was a clean tackle
The defender broke the rules badly

payload.translation: Lee is praising the defender for making a smart calculated foul to prevent a dangerous counter-attack.

followUps.line: Would you take that yellow in that situation?
Do you think VAR should review it?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Tactical fouls are legal; they're just a cost-benefit decision players make.

lessons.title: Last man: DOGSO
lessons.objective: You can explain when a foul is a red card because it denied a goal chance.

payload.prompt: The last defender brings down an attacker clean through. What card?

situation.narrative: The attacker has the ball under control and is racing toward goal.

facts.label: Defenders
facts.value: The fouler is the last one back

facts.label: Foul
facts.value: Trip from behind, no attempt at the ball

options.label: Red card for denying an obvious goal-scoring opportunity
options.consequence: Correct. The defender is sent off and the attacking side gets a direct free kick.
considerations: Distance and direction of play favour a goal
The foul is a trip, not a genuine attempt to play the ball

options.label: Yellow card for a normal foul
options.consequence: That undersells it. The defender has removed a clear chance and keeps playing.
considerations: A yellow fits when the chance is not obvious
Here the attacker had a clear route to goal

options.label: Free kick only, no card
options.consequence: A free kick alone would let a defender stop a certain goal and pay almost nothing.
considerations: Denying a goal chance always carries a card

payload.expertNote: Referees run the four Ds: distance to goal, direction of play, defenders who can recover, and control of the ball. Outside the box a foul that denies a goal chance is red even if the defender makes a challenge for the ball.
payload.sayThisLine: Last man, clean through, that's DOGSO.

payload.prompt: Just outside the box, the last defender clips an attacker clean through while trying for the ball. Card?

options.text: Red, because outside the area a trying-for-the-ball foul is still DOGSO
Yellow, because he tried to play the ball
No card, because he tried to win it

explanation.correct: Right. Outside the penalty area, a foul that denies an obvious goal chance is a red card even if the defender genuinely tried to play the ball. The lighter yellow only applies inside the box.
explanation.incorrect: The 'he went for the ball' reduction to yellow only applies inside the penalty area, where the attacker also gets a penalty. Outside the box, denying the goal chance is red.
explanation.sayThisLine: Outside the box it's a red, even if he went for the ball.

payload.prompt: A covering defender is right behind the last man, who fouls an attacker. Is it DOGSO red?

scene.alt: An attacker is heading toward goal with a defender fouling him, but a second defender is close enough to recover and challenge.

explanation.correct: No. With a second defender close enough to get back and challenge, the chance is not obvious, so it is a foul that usually earns a yellow, not a DOGSO red.
explanation.incorrect: DOGSO needs an obvious chance. A covering defender who can recover means it is not obvious, so the foul is normally a yellow for stopping a promising attack.
explanation.sayThisLine: Someone was covering, so it's not DOGSO. Yellow at most.

payload.prompt: A defender pulls back a clean-through striker by the shirt inside the area, no attempt to play the ball. Punishment?

options.text: Penalty and red card
Penalty and yellow card
Just a penalty, no card

explanation.correct: Right. Denying an obvious goal-scoring opportunity with a foul that is not a genuine attempt to play the ball, such as holding or pulling, is a penalty and a red card.
explanation.incorrect: Holding or pulling is not an attempt to play the ball, so the referee awards a penalty and sends the defender off. The yellow-card version only applies when the defender genuinely challenges for the ball.
explanation.sayThisLine: He pulled him back in the box: penalty and red.

payload.prompt: The keeper races outside his area and brings down an attacker clean through. Red card?

scene.alt: A goalkeeper has left his penalty area and fouls an attacker who is clear through on goal.

explanation.correct: Yes. DOGSO applies to any defender, including the goalkeeper. Outside the area the keeper is treated like any outfield player.
explanation.incorrect: The goalkeeper is a defender too. Fouling an attacker clean through outside the box denies an obvious goal chance and is a red card.
explanation.sayThisLine: Keeper's outside the box, clean through: red card.

payload.prompt: An attacker is 35 yards out with two defenders goal-side when he is fouled. DOGSO?

options.text: Yes, any foul on a runner is DOGSO
No, he is too far out and defenders can still get back
Only if he is on his stronger foot

explanation.correct: Right. Distance to goal and the number of defenders who can recover both count against it being an obvious goal chance. It is a foul, but probably not a red.
explanation.incorrect: Referees weigh distance to goal, direction of play, defenders and control of the ball. At 35 yards with two defenders back, the chance is not obvious.
explanation.sayThisLine: Too far out and covered, so no DOGSO.

lessons.title: Handball, the eternal argument
lessons.objective: You can explain why some handballs are penalties and some are not.

payload.prompt: A defender sees the ball coming and holds out an arm to block it. Handball?

scene.alt: A defender deliberately extends an arm to block or stop a shot or pass heading toward goal.

explanation.correct: Yes. Deliberately extending an arm to block the ball is handball, whatever the distance.
explanation.incorrect: Intent is clear when a player sticks an arm out to stop the ball. That is handball, a direct free kick or a penalty in the box.
explanation.sayThisLine: He put his arm out on purpose, that's handball.

payload.prompt: A cross hits a defender's arm, which is tucked close to his body. Is it handball?

options.text: Yes, any contact with the arm is handball
No, an arm in a natural position close to the body is not an offence
Only if the ball was heading for the goal

explanation.correct: Right. The question is whether the player made his body unnaturally bigger. An arm tucked in at his side is in a natural position, so it is not handball.
explanation.incorrect: Handball is not simply arm-touches-ball. The referee asks whether the arm made the body unnaturally bigger or was deliberately moved to the ball. Tucked in is natural.
explanation.sayThisLine: Arm at the side, probably okay. Arm out, probably handball.

payload.prompt: A defender's arm is at his side. The ball ricochets off his hip and hits his arm by accident. Handball?

scene.alt: A ball deflects unexpectedly and strikes a defender's arm that is in a natural position at the body; contact is incidental.

explanation.correct: No. Accidental contact with the arm in a natural position is not handball.
explanation.incorrect: If the arm is in a natural position and the contact is not deliberate, it is not an offence.
explanation.sayThisLine: Arm at the side, ball hits it by chance, that's not handball.

payload.prompt: The ball hits a player's shoulder. Handball?

scene.alt: A cross strikes a defender on the shoulder, just above the arm.

explanation.correct: No. The shoulder is not part of the arm for handball purposes. The arm is judged from the bottom of the armpit down.
explanation.incorrect: The upper boundary of the arm is the bottom of the armpit, so shoulder contact is never handball.
explanation.sayThisLine: Shoulder's not the arm, that's not handball.

statement.speaker: Casey
statement.text: His arm made his body bigger, that should be a handball penalty.

payload.question: What is Casey saying?

options.text: The player's arm was in an unnatural position
The enlarged body meant handball
It was accidental so not handball
The arm did not touch the ball

payload.translation: Casey is arguing that the player's arm was not in a natural position, making his body unnaturally bigger, which is handball.

followUps.line: Did the arm move or was it always out there?
followUps.why: Tests understanding of movement vs position.

followUps.line: Would you call that if it was a defender vs a striker?
followUps.why: Notes that handball is applied consistently.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Handball is the most argued rule; both sides usually have a point.

payload.prompt: A defender handles the ball inside his own area. What is the restart?

scene.alt: A defender commits a handball offence inside his own penalty area.

explanation.correct: Right. A handball offence by the defending team inside its own penalty area is punished with a penalty kick.
explanation.incorrect: A direct free kick is the restart outside the box. Inside the defender's own area the handball becomes a penalty kick.
explanation.sayThisLine: Handball in the box, straight to the spot.

lessons.title: Diving and dissent
lessons.objective: You can explain why simulation and dissent get cautions.

payload.prompt: A player is lightly brushed and falls down dramatically to win a free kick. What is this?

options.text: A foul on the player
Simulation, a dive; a yellow card
Advantage to the fouled player

explanation.correct: Right. Exaggerating or faking contact to win a free kick is simulation and a yellow.
explanation.incorrect: Simulation is pretending to be fouled when you are not, or exaggerating minor contact. It is an offence.
explanation.sayThisLine: He went down easy, that's a dive, yellow card.

payload.prompt: After the ref makes a call, a player yells 'That was wrong!' and argues with him. Yellow card?

scene.alt: A player loudly disputes a referee decision by arguing or complaining; the player is clearly challenging the referee's authority.

explanation.correct: Yes. Arguing with the referee or abusing him is dissent, a yellow card.
explanation.incorrect: Dissent, arguing with or abusing the referee, is an automatic yellow card offence.
explanation.sayThisLine: Can't argue with the ref, that's a yellow.

payload.prompt: Several players crowd the referee shouting about a decision. What is he likely to do?

options.text: Let it go, emotions are part of football
Caution the loudest for dissent and ask the captain to calm things down
Send the whole team off

explanation.correct: Right. The captain has no special powers, but referees lean on him to keep the group calm. Crowding and shouting at the referee is dissent and can be cautioned.
explanation.incorrect: Referees do not tolerate crowding and shouting, but they do not send off a whole team either. The usual answer is a caution for the worst offender and a word with the captain.
explanation.sayThisLine: Only the captain should be talking to the ref.

statement.speaker: Mo
statement.text: He touched him but he went down too easy. That should be a yellow.

payload.question: What does Mo mean?

options.text: The contact was minimal but the player exaggerated
It should be a yellow for simulation or diving
It should be a free kick
The player was seriously fouled

payload.translation: Mo is saying the player exaggerated minor contact to deceive the referee, which is simulation and should be a yellow.

followUps.line: Do you think he went down too easy?
followUps.why: Tests your reading of the contact.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Diving is a judgment call; watch the contact and the fall together.

payload.prompt: A player shoves a referee after an argument. Is he sent off?

scene.alt: A player makes physical contact with a referee, pushing or touching him in aggression.

explanation.correct: Yes. Touching or pushing a referee is violent conduct, a straight red.
explanation.incorrect: Any physical contact with an official is violent conduct and a direct red card.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hands on the ref, that's violent conduct, straight red.

lessons.title: The officials and the keeper's rules
lessons.objective: You can name the officials and explain the back-pass and eight-second rules.

payload.prompt: Match the official to the job.

pairs.definition: The main official who makes decisions, blows the whistle and issues cards.
Two officials on the touchlines who flag for out-of-play and offside decisions.
At the bench who manages substitutions, replacement balls and keeps time.
In a room with screens who can recommend reviews for serious errors.

explanation.summary: Five officials: ref, two assistants on the lines, fourth at the bench, and VAR in a room.
explanation.sayThisLine: One ref, two assistants, fourth official, and VAR.

payload.prompt: A teammate deliberately kicks the ball back to the goalkeeper and he catches it. What does the referee do?

options.text: Nothing, he is allowed to do that
Gives an indirect free kick to the other team
Gives a penalty

explanation.correct: Right. A keeper cannot handle a deliberate back-pass; an indirect free kick is given.
explanation.incorrect: The back-pass rule forbids the keeper from handling the ball if a teammate deliberately kicks it to him.
explanation.sayThisLine: Can't pick up a back-pass, he has to use his feet.

payload.prompt: Tap the moment the keeper's eight seconds run out.

explanation.correct: Sharp. A keeper who holds the ball too long concedes a corner, and the referee counts down the last five seconds with a raised hand.
explanation.incorrect: A keeper who controls the ball in his hands for more than eight seconds concedes a corner. The referee raises a hand to count the last five seconds.
explanation.sayThisLine: He held it too long, that's a corner.

payload.prompt: Complete the free-kick distance rule.
payload.template: At a free kick the defending wall must stand at least {{yards}} yards ({{metres}} metres) from the ball.

explanation.correct: Right. Ten yards, which is 9.15 metres, is the minimum distance for the wall.
explanation.incorrect: The wall must be at least 10 yards (9.15 metres) from the ball until it is kicked. Referees often use vanishing spray to mark the line.
explanation.sayThisLine: The wall has to be ten yards back, standard.

payload.prompt: A teammate throws the ball in to the goalkeeper. Can he pick it up?

options.text: Yes, only kicks count for the back-pass rule
No, the back-pass rule covers throw-ins too
Only if he is outside his box

explanation.correct: Right. A keeper cannot handle the ball after a teammate deliberately kicks it to him, or after receiving it directly from a teammate's throw-in. An indirect free kick follows.
explanation.incorrect: The back-pass rule covers a deliberate kick and also a throw-in from a teammate straight to the keeper. If he handles it, the opponents get an indirect free kick.
explanation.sayThisLine: A throw-in straight to the keeper counts as a back-pass too.

payload.prompt: What does the fourth official do during the match?

options.text: Makes offside calls on the touchline
Manages substitutions, replacement balls and timekeeping
Reviews VAR decisions

explanation.correct: Right. The fourth manages the bench, subs and equipment.
explanation.incorrect: The fourth official stands at the bench, manages substitutions, keeps time and handles spare balls.
explanation.sayThisLine: Fourth official is at the bench, handles the subs and the ball.

lessons.title: Time-wasting crackdown
lessons.objective: You can explain the new restart countdown and injury rules.

payload.prompt: A team drags out a throw-in and the ref begins the five-second countdown. If it runs out?

options.text: The ref waits a little longer
The throw-in goes to the other team
The ref shows a red card

explanation.correct: Right. If the countdown runs out, the throw-in is given to the opponents. For a slow goal kick, the opponents get a corner instead.
explanation.incorrect: The countdown is a real deadline. When the five seconds expire, the restart is taken away: a throw-in goes to the other team and a goal kick becomes a corner.
explanation.sayThisLine: Five seconds, then the throw goes to the other side.

payload.prompt: A treated player is ready to go straight back on. Can he?

situation.narrative: A midfielder has received treatment on the pitch after a tackle, and play has been stopped for a while.

options.label: He leaves the pitch and waits at least one minute
options.consequence: The team plays a player short for that minute, which discourages using treatment as a time-out.
considerations: The rule aims to stop feigned injuries wasting time
A minimum of one minute off the pitch

options.label: He stays on because he says he is fine
options.consequence: The referee sends him off the pitch; the rule is applied regardless of how he feels.
considerations: It is the referee's call, not the player's

options.label: Bring a substitute on instead, so the team is not short
options.consequence: Possible, but it uses one of the team's substitutions, so it is a real cost.
considerations: The team's aim is to stay at eleven

payload.expertNote: The rule targets the tactical use of injury treatment to slow the game. Genuine injuries still get treated immediately, and the referee can deal with real concussion cases separately under the medical protocols.
payload.sayThisLine: He's been treated, so he has to wait a minute to come back.

payload.prompt: A goalkeeper takes ages over a goal kick and the ref starts the countdown. If it runs out?

options.text: The keeper gets one more warning
The opponents get a corner kick
The referee awards a penalty

explanation.correct: Right. A goal kick that is not taken within the five-second countdown gives the opponents a corner. It is a big penalty for a small delay.
explanation.incorrect: The countdown has real teeth. When a goal kick delay runs out the five seconds, the opponents get a corner kick.
explanation.sayThisLine: Take the goal kick or they get a corner.

payload.prompt: A substituted player strolls off. Should he hurry to avoid a penalty for delay?

scene.alt: A player is being replaced and walks slowly toward the touchline instead of leaving promptly.

explanation.correct: Yes. In 2026/27 the substituted player is expected to leave within ten seconds, so a slow walk off can delay the substitute coming on.
explanation.incorrect: Substitutions are part of the time-wasting crackdown. A player who takes his time can hold up the replacement, so leaving quickly is the safe move.
explanation.sayThisLine: Off you go, ten seconds, that's all you get.

payload.prompt: A player has been treated on the pitch and wants to carry on right away. What is the 2026/27 rule?

options.text: He can stay if he feels okay
He leaves the pitch and can only return after a minute
His team receives an extra substitution

explanation.correct: Right. After on-pitch treatment the player generally has to leave for at least a minute, which discourages delaying the game with a fake injury. A few exceptions exist, so check the current Laws.
explanation.incorrect: The 2026/27 change asks a treated player to leave the field for a minute before coming back, a way to stop injuries being used to waste time.
explanation.sayThisLine: Treatment on the pitch means a minute off, then back on.
